## Monterrey, Mexico: modern districts and the Sierra Madre mountains

Monterrey is the capital of Nuevo León state in northeastern [Mexico](/mexico/). Rocky mountains surround the city, whose history is closely connected with industry, trade and contemporary culture. Here you can combine city museums, historic public spaces and outings on nature trails.

Monterrey is markedly different from [Oaxaca](/mexico/place/oaxaca/) and [Morelia](/mexico/place/morelia/), where visitors often explore colonial neighborhoods before visiting museums. Monterrey's defining feature is the proximity of a large modern metropolitan area to steep slopes and canyons. To appreciate the contrast, allow one day for the center and another for nature.

## Macroplaza, museums and the old center

Macroplaza is a large central public space with green areas and well-known civic buildings. It is home to the striking Faro del Comercio, and nearby museums focus on the region's history. A walk through the center reveals modern city landmarks alongside earlier monuments.

Nearby Barrio Antiguo is home to historic buildings, cafes and cultural venues. It fits conveniently into the same walking itinerary without spending the day driving back and forth. Museum admission arrangements and event schedules change, so check opening hours before choosing an exhibition.

## Fundidora Park and the Santa Lucía canal

Fundidora Park occupies the site of a former steelworks. Preserved industrial structures recall Monterrey's development as a major manufacturing center. Today the area has walking paths, cultural venues and spaces for sport and relaxation.

The Santa Lucía canal connects the Macroplaza area with Fundidora. Park authorities describe the waterway as approximately 2.5 km long. You can walk alongside it to see the urban surroundings or check whether boat rides are operating. For a first visit, it is a good way to connect museums and the park within one day.

In hot weather, plan outdoor walks for the morning and evening, leaving the middle of the day for air-conditioned indoor attractions.

## Mountains around Monterrey: Chipinque and La Huasteca

Chipinque Park attracts visitors with forest trails and views across the city. The La Huasteca natural area is known for towering limestone walls, gorges and rock-climbing opportunities. Other caves and canyons are found nearby, but their routes demand very different levels of fitness.

For a casual walk, choose officially open trails. Rock climbing, canyon descents and demanding treks require appropriate training, equipment and a qualified specialist. Summer heat and changes in the weather can make some routes unsafe; check restrictions imposed by the protected area's management before setting out.

If you enjoy these activities, explore [adventure journeys](/interests/adventure/), but do not confuse outdoor pursuits around Monterrey with sightseeing excursions within the city.

## How many days should you allow for Monterrey?

Set aside one full city day for Macroplaza, the Santa Lucía canal, museums and Fundidora Park. An additional day is needed if you plan to explore the mountains. More demanding outdoor activities take as long as the chosen route and guide's instructions require.

Our catalog does not currently include a separate active itinerary with a guaranteed visit to Monterrey. Specific excursions, transport and accommodation arrangements therefore need to be agreed individually, without assuming any services are included.

## Frequently asked questions about Monterrey

### Can I enjoy Monterrey without mountain hikes?

Yes. Macroplaza, museums, the Santa Lucía canal, Fundidora Park and historic neighborhoods provide a complete city itinerary without strenuous climbs.

### What is best to see in one day?

Start with the center and Macroplaza, then walk along the Santa Lucía canal to Fundidora Park. Allow time for museums according to their actual opening hours.

### Can I explore La Huasteca independently?

For walks, use only permitted routes you can navigate confidently. Technical climbing and canyoning require experience, equipment and qualified guidance.

## Morelia: pink stone and a historic Mexican city center

Morelia, the capital of Michoacán state, lies in central [Mexico](/mexico/). Its historic center is known for buildings of pink cantera stone, colonial squares, arcades and churches. UNESCO inscribed the old city on the World Heritage List in 1991, recognizing its well-preserved layout and architecture.

Unlike the large modern city of [Monterrey](/mexico/place/monterrey/), Morelia is particularly attractive for a leisurely walk through its historic core. You can move between several monuments on foot and see how the city's architectural styles changed over time.

## The cathedral and central squares

Morelia Cathedral, with its tall towers, is one of the city's major architectural landmarks. Its facade and interior express the traditions of colonial Baroque, and the surrounding area forms a natural starting point for exploring the city.

According to UNESCO, Morelia's historic center contains more than 200 exceptional buildings, many constructed from the region's characteristic pink stone. Monuments from different periods include churches, monasteries, civic buildings and arcades. Walking through the streets reveals a combination of Renaissance, Baroque and Neoclassical elements.

To appreciate the architecture, do more than photograph the main cathedral. Walk through nearby streets and lanes: smaller squares and courtyards often reveal the city's atmosphere better than isolated monuments.

## The aqueduct and the Shrine of Guadalupe

Morelia's historic aqueduct stretches through the urban landscape. It recalls the development of the city's water supply and provides another perspective beyond the main square.

The Shrine of Our Lady of Guadalupe is known for its elaborate decoration. It is often included in walking routes alongside the aqueduct and other religious landmarks. Respect services in active churches and observe current photography rules; check restrictions and visiting hours locally.

For a full city day, a combination of the cathedral, central streets, aqueduct and one or two museums is usually more rewarding than trying to visit every church.

## Morelia and the history of Mexican independence

The city was formerly called Valladolid. It received its present name in honor of José María Morelos, one of the most important leaders in Mexico's independence struggle, who was born here. Historic buildings therefore tell stories both of Spanish colonial heritage and of the formation of the Mexican state.

UNESCO emphasizes Morelia's significance to the country's architecture and political history. A local expert's tour can be particularly useful if you want to connect specific buildings with historical events.

## Planning a visit

Morelia is best treated as a cultural destination in its own right, rather than a brief photo stop between distant cities. One day allows you to explore the main streets and monuments; consider staying overnight if you want to visit museums and walk at a relaxed pace.

For comparison, look at [San Miguel de Allende](/mexico/place/san-miguel-de-allende/) and [Guanajuato](/mexico/place/guanajuato/). Both are notable for their architecture but have distinct urban landscapes and histories. Consider the distances between them and transport availability.

At present, our catalog does not confirm a visit to Morelia on a specific published tour. A trip here requires individual planning of the route, excursions and accommodation.

## Frequently asked questions about Morelia

### Why is Morelia called the pink city?

Many historic buildings were constructed from local pink cantera stone. This material gives the streets their distinctive hue and unifies the historic center's appearance.

### What part of Morelia is UNESCO-listed?

The historic center of Morelia, inscribed in 1991. The designation covers its urban layout, squares and numerous buildings from different periods.

### Is Morelia suitable for a walking tour?

Yes. The main landmarks in the historic center are fairly close together. Additional museums and more distant attractions take extra time and sometimes require transport.

## National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City: what to see and how to plan your visit

The National Museum of Anthropology (Museo Nacional de Antropología) is located near [Chapultepec Park](/mexico/place/chapultepec/) in [Mexico City](/mexico/). It houses archaeological objects from ancient civilizations and ethnographic collections relating to peoples living in Mexico today. It is an excellent introduction to Mesoamerican history: after a visit, ruins, city squares and the names of ancient cultures become parts of a larger story rather than unrelated attractions.

The museum building is also worth seeing. Its modern complex opened in 1964, following a design led by architect Pedro Ramírez Vázquez. The galleries face a central courtyard, and visitors are free to choose the order in which they explore them.

## Which galleries should you choose on a first visit?

Plan your time around your interests rather than trying to rush through every collection without stopping.

- **Mexica culture.** This gallery contains the famous Sun Stone, often called the Aztec calendar. Nearby objects offer a clearer understanding of the symbolism, religious beliefs and political history of the empire centered on Tenochtitlan.
- **Teotihuacán.** Artifacts from the ancient city help prepare you to visit the archaeological site, connecting monumental architecture with ceramics, representations of deities and everyday objects.
- **Maya culture.** Sculptures, reliefs and inscriptions demonstrate why the history of Maya cities is studied through monuments to their rulers and their rituals.
- **Cultures of Oaxaca and the Gulf Coast.** These collections show that Mexico's pre-Hispanic history extends well beyond any single people or capital.
- **Ethnographic collections.** They connect the archaeological past with the languages, crafts and traditions of present-day communities.

If the development of the capital particularly interests you, start with the Mexica gallery, then visit the discoveries at [Templo Mayor](/mexico/place/templo-mayor/) in the historic center. These are two ways to experience the same era: the museum supplies the broader context, while the archaeological site reveals the actual location of the ancient city.

## El Paraguas: why step into the courtyard?

At the heart of the museum complex stands **El Paraguas**, "the Umbrella": a vast overhanging roof supported by a bronze-covered column with cascading water. It is an architectural symbol of the museum and a convenient place to pause between galleries. The column's decoration features images from Mexico's history and cultures.

The courtyard is laid out so visitors can move between exhibitions without following a single compulsory path. You can therefore divide your visit into manageable sections: two or three galleries, a short pause by the water and another group of exhibits chosen according to your interests.

## How much time should you allow?

**Plan roughly two to three hours to see the main displays, or half a day for a more thoughtful exploration of several cultures and ethnographic galleries.** These are planning guidelines, not durations prescribed by the museum.

| Time available | What you can see |
|---|---|
| 1–1.5 hours | One main gallery and the courtyard |
| 2–3 hours | Mexica and one or two additional themes |
| Half a day | Several cultures and ethnographic exhibitions |

The quantity of information can be more tiring than walking around. If you are visiting with children, choose a handful of impressive exhibits and tell stories about them instead of moving mechanically from display case to display case.

## Where the museum is and how to combine it with Mexico City

The museum is on Paseo de la Reforma, near Chapultepec Park. You can continue walking nearby, but reaching monuments in the city center requires a separate transfer.

For a day devoted to ancient history, a logical combination is "Museum of Anthropology → [Templo Mayor](/mexico/place/templo-mayor/)". To experience different periods of Mexico City, combine the museum with the [Zócalo](/mexico/place/mexico-city-zocalo/) and the [Metropolitan Cathedral](/mexico/place/mexico-city-metropolitan-cathedral/). A multi-stop route through the capital is available in the [Zócalo, Chapultepec and Anthropology Museum excursion](/mexico/mexico-city-and-teotihuacan/mexico-city-zocalo-chapultepec-anthropology/).

Another approach is to explore the cultures of ancient Mexico in the museum first, then take an archaeological excursion on a different day. In this case, the museum introduces the sites rather than replacing the experience of seeing the monuments in person.

## What to check before visiting

The museum is administered by INAH, Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History. It normally opens Tuesday through Sunday; verify the schedule, accessibility of individual galleries and admission prices on the museum's official website just before traveling. Temporary closures and special exhibitions may affect your visit.

When choosing an excursion, ask how much time is allocated specifically to the displays: mentioning the museum on an itinerary may mean a brief stop or an in-depth visit. On [cultural tours of Mexico](/mexico/tour/), the museum is particularly valuable as an introduction to historic sites elsewhere in the country.

## Frequently asked questions about the Museum of Anthropology

### Where is the National Museum of Anthropology?

In Mexico City, near Chapultepec Park on Paseo de la Reforma. It is a large national museum, not a museum attached to any one archaeological site.

### Can I see the museum in one hour?

You can choose one gallery and visit the courtyard, but you will not see the main collection in an hour. Allow two to three hours for a meaningful first visit.

### How does it differ from Templo Mayor?

The Museum of Anthropology covers numerous civilizations and living ethnographic traditions. [Templo Mayor](/mexico/place/templo-mayor/) is associated with the remains of the main temple complex of ancient Tenochtitlan.

### Is the museum interesting if I've already visited the pyramids?

Yes. Sculpture, everyday objects and explanations of religious scenes reveal details that are difficult to understand from the architectural remains at outdoor sites.

### Do I need to buy a ticket in advance?

Ticket prices and sales procedures can change. Check the current purchase arrangements and opening hours directly on the official INAH resource.

## Which Ada Tours itineraries visit the National Museum of Anthropology?

We offer {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} with the [National Museum of Anthropology](/mexico/place/national-museum-of-anthropology/) as a required stop. The museum is in Mexico City, near [Chapultepec](/mexico/place/chapultepec/). Its archaeological and ethnographic collections help visitors understand Mexican culture from ancient civilizations to the present.

On the [seven-day Religious Journey through Mexico](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/), the museum is visited on day two. The current tour is scheduled for April 1–7, 2027, and April 2 combines the [Guadalupe](/mexico/place/basilica-of-guadalupe/) shrine with the anthropology museum. Other days include churches and sacred sites in central Mexico, [Teotihuacán](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/) and additional attractions.

On the [Central America: Eight Countries in 26 Days tour](/multi-country/tour/central-america-8-countries-26-days/), the National Museum of Anthropology is part of the Mexico City sightseeing itinerary on day two. The program also includes the historic center, [Zócalo](/mexico/place/mexico-city-zocalo/), Metropolitan Cathedral, [Templo Mayor](/mexico/place/templo-mayor/) and [Chapultepec](/mexico/place/chapultepec/). The journey then continues to Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Panama.

| Itinerary | Role of the museum |
|---|---|
| [Mexico, seven days](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/) | History alongside a pilgrimage program |
| [Eight countries, 26 days](/multi-country/tour/central-america-8-countries-26-days/) | Introduction to Mesoamerican civilizations |

{{catalog.tourTable:tour_mexico_religious_journey,tour_central_america_eight_countries_26_days}}

The two journeys serve different purposes. In the first, the museum complements an itinerary exploring religious heritage. In the second, it provides background on pre-Columbian history before travelers visit ancient sites in other Central American countries. This selection does not include a separate multi-day museum-only tour.

## What can you see in the museum, and why does it matter for the journey?

The National Museum of Anthropology is part of Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH). The current building opened in 1964. Its permanent archaeological and ethnographic collections contain both material evidence of ancient cultures and objects reflecting the traditions of Indigenous peoples in modern Mexico.

Visitors often begin in the archaeological galleries. Exhibitions cover Teotihuacán, Mexica culture, Maya heritage and the different regions of Mesoamerica, including Oaxaca. Sculptures, stone reliefs, ceramics, ornaments and other discoveries are on display. Many artifacts are easier to appreciate if you have already visited their associated sites or will explore them later on the journey.

The ethnographic collections continue the story through living communities. Clothing, crafts, household objects and traditions reveal the cultural diversity of present-day Mexico. This is particularly valuable to travelers who otherwise associate Mexican history mainly with pyramids.

One of the building's most recognizable features stands in the central courtyard: El Paraguas, an enormous canopy supported by a central column with water flowing around it. Its architecture has become a symbol of the museum. The courtyard provides a welcome pause between information-rich galleries, although exploring the collections thoroughly takes far longer than viewing this landmark.

For an independent overview of the museum and its cultural importance, see the [museum destination page](/mexico/place/national-museum-of-anthropology/). Here we focus on the museum as a stop on actual itineraries and how the two travel formats shape the experience.

## The museum on a seven-day religious journey through Mexico

The [seven-day itinerary](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/) is designed around pilgrimage and historic churches. On **April 2, 2027**, it includes the [Shrine of Our Lady of Guadalupe](/mexico/place/basilica-of-guadalupe/), participation in Mass and a visit to the National Museum of Anthropology. As one of the first days of the route, the museum provides cultural and historical context for subsequent excursions.

During the week, travelers discover religious sites in Mexico City, Tlaxcala, Ocotlán, Puebla and other parts of central Mexico. The tour includes six nights in Mexico City, an English-speaking guide, and breakfasts and dinners under this program's terms. Its dates and schedule of religious observances belong specifically to this product and should not automatically be applied to other cultural itineraries.

Do not confuse this museum visit with a dedicated in-depth guided exploration of all its galleries. The shrine and museum share the same day, so time is divided between them. If studying archaeological and ethnographic displays is your primary aim, mention that when arranging a personalized itinerary. Spending additional time at the museum would require changing the sequence of the day's visits.

This option suits those principally interested in religious history and Catholic holy sites, with the museum adding to their understanding of the country's wider culture. The full schedule of services, excursion durations and payment terms appear on the [religious tour page](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/).

## The museum on a journey through eight Central American countries

On the [26-day itinerary](/multi-country/tour/central-america-8-countries-26-days/), the museum is scheduled for **day two**, devoted to Mexico City's historic neighborhoods. One full sightseeing day combines [Zócalo](/mexico/place/mexico-city-zocalo/), the cathedral, [Templo Mayor](/mexico/place/templo-mayor/), [Chapultepec](/mexico/place/chapultepec/) and the Museum of Anthropology. The tour takes place with an English-speaking guide. This is an intensive introduction to the capital, not a promise of an entire day inside the museum.

After Mexico, the itinerary reaches other countries, including Belize, Guatemala and Honduras, with monuments of Maya civilization, followed by natural and cultural attractions in southern Central America. Early in the trip, the museum introduces Mesoamerica's chronology, geography and artistic traditions, making it easier to recognize familiar themes at actual archaeological complexes later.

This format is particularly rewarding for first-time visitors to the region. Rather than studying each museum display in detail, travelers gain a broad overview that the visits to different countries subsequently reinforce. The overall pace is more demanding, however: more flights and road transfers, changes of accommodation and long sightseeing days.

Including the museum does not make the 26-day itinerary a trip devoted exclusively to Mexican history. It covers eight countries, so priorities are best set in the context of the entire route. For specifics, see the [full Central America program](/multi-country/tour/central-america-8-countries-26-days/).

## What to look for when comparing the two programs

To choose between them, first ask why you want to visit this particular museum.

If you want to study Mexico's religious history and combine its collections with a visit to the Guadalupe shrine, the seven-day program is closer to your interests. If your aim is a major journey across Mesoamerica and tropical Central America, the museum on the 26-day trip supplies a useful historical foundation.

In both cases, the museum is in a large city and scheduled on a busy second day. Several hours are needed to explore the galleries thoughtfully. Visitors with a special interest in archaeology should name their priorities in advance: cultures of the Valley of Mexico, the Maya or Oaxaca. Otherwise, seeing the collections can become an overly hurried walk.

A museum visit should also be distinguished from an independent visit to an archaeological monument. The museum houses original objects and scientific explanations, while [Teotihuacán](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/) reveals the layout of an actual ancient city. These complementary experiences require different amounts of time and visiting arrangements.

When comparing prices, use only the published terms of each specific product. The current catalog does not confirm a numerical price for the religious tour. The multi-country journey has its own service inclusions, flight arrangements and accommodation terms. They cannot be combined into an imaginary "museum visit package" or assumed to include identical tickets and guidance.

## Practical aspects of visiting the National Museum of Anthropology

The museum is on Paseo de la Reforma next to [Chapultepec Park](/mexico/place/chapultepec/). INAH publishes independent admission rules, opening hours, photography restrictions and temporary exhibition schedules. At the time of the source review, the museum was open Tuesday through Sunday; **Monday is normally its closing day**. Check current information before an independent visit, especially if travel dates change.

The complex contains many galleries, with substantial distances between them. It is better to choose a few sections and give them sufficient time than to attempt a quick tour of everything. The museum's official website lists accessibility assistance, including wheelchairs on request, for people who have difficulty walking or standing for long periods. Discuss specific needs in advance when planning a group visit.

Personal photography is permitted without flash. Tripods and additional lighting are prohibited under INAH rules. Exhibitions can change and some rooms may close temporarily, so a tour description should promise a general museum visit rather than a guaranteed view of a specific artifact in an exact location.

You will gain more from the museum if you know which themes matter most to the rest of your journey: Aztec and Teotihuacán history, Maya heritage, cultures of Oaxaca or the ethnography of modern Mexico. A guide can help relate museum exhibits to places you will visit later, but the galleries selected and the duration must fit the confirmed itinerary.

## What if the museum is the main purpose of the trip?

If you have a strong interest in the museum and ancient history, start by comparing [culture-and-history trips](/interests/culture-and-history/) and [Mexico itineraries](/mexico/tour/). You can choose according to the number of days in Mexico City and surrounding sites, but only routes explicitly listing the museum confirm that it is included.

To explore the theme further, see [Teotihuacán](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/), [Templo Mayor](/mexico/place/templo-mayor/), [Zócalo](/mexico/place/mexico-city-zocalo/) and [Chapultepec](/mexico/place/chapultepec/). Together, these places help you create a custom sightseeing route around the museum, taking city travel times into account.

If you are planning a major journey across Central America, it is more useful to see the museum as an introduction to a long historical and nature-focused trip. Compare departure dates, rest between transfers and actual excursions each day. The museum will then become a meaningful beginning to the region rather than an incidental brief stop.

## Frequently asked questions about tours visiting the National Museum of Anthropology

### On which day is the museum scheduled?

It is on day two of both active itineraries. On the seven-day religious tour this means April 2, 2027; on the 26-day Central America route, it is the second day after arriving in Mexico City.

### Can I spend a full day at the museum?

Both published itineraries combine the museum with other attractions on the same day. A full museum day is not confirmed as part of either package. An extended visit must be agreed as a change to an individualized itinerary.

### Is the museum suitable for a first trip to Mexico?

Yes, especially for travelers interested in history and culture. Archaeological exhibits introduce Mesoamerican civilizations before a visit to the ancient cities themselves.

### Can I photograph the exhibits?

Official rules permit personal photography without flash, tripods or additional lighting. Temporary exhibitions may have separate restrictions, so follow the instructions of museum staff.

### Which program is better if I'm interested in ancient civilizations?

For a broad introduction to Mesoamerica and Central American countries, the [26-day itinerary](/multi-country/tour/central-america-8-countries-26-days/) is a better fit. The [seven-day tour](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/) primarily focuses on religion and includes a museum visit.

### Is the museum outside Mexico City?

No. It is within Mexico City near Chapultepec. It is an urban attraction, usually combined with other sights in the capital.

## National Palace, Mexico City: Diego Rivera's murals and Mexican history

**The National Palace (Palacio Nacional)** stands in the historic center of [Mexico City](/mexico/place/mexico-city-and-teotihuacan/), occupying the eastern side of the [Zócalo](/mexico/place/mexico-city-zocalo/). Its long facade, central entrance and national flag are recognizable even on an ordinary walk across the square. The palace has been a seat of government through several historical periods and remains a government complex today.

The principal attraction of its interiors is Diego Rivera's monumental murals, in which the artist presented his own interpretation of Mexican history. However, **viewing the palace from the square and visiting its interior are different experiences**: admission depends on the schedule of official events and current registration rules.

## From Moctezuma's palace to the seat of government

Before the Spanish conquest, this site contained the so-called New Houses of Moctezuma, the ruler of Tenochtitlan. After the conquest, the land passed into the control of Hernán Cortés and subsequently the Spanish Crown. The buildings were expanded, adapted to the administration of the viceroyalty and reconstructed several times.

The palace acquired its present appearance over several centuries. A third floor was added to the complex in the early 20th century, so the building visible from the Zócalo combines older history with later architectural alterations.

Nearby stands [Templo Mayor](/mexico/place/templo-mayor/), the principal temple of ancient Tenochtitlan. Comparing the palace with the excavations helps explain how the city's political center changed, although they are separate attractions with distinct access arrangements.

## What do Diego Rivera's murals depict?

The palace's best-known work is **The Epic of the Mexican People**, painted on the walls of the grand staircase. Diego Rivera worked on it from 1929 to 1935. In this expansive, multi-figure narrative, he combined pre-Hispanic cultures, the colonial period, the struggle for independence and revolutionary events.

This is the artist's interpretation of history, not a neutral illustrated chronology. Rivera emphasized different figures and events in keeping with his artistic and political convictions. It is particularly interesting to notice whom he places at the center of each scene, which historical conflicts he portrays and how he represents everyday life.

Rivera returned to work at the palace in the 1940s. Murals on the upper gallery walls portray Mesoamerican cultures and encounters between Indigenous peoples and the Spanish. Allow time to study the paintings: small details and figures' labels are difficult to appreciate during a hurried visit.

## Can visitors enter the National Palace?

Mexican official sources describe **guided visits requiring advance registration**, with entrance procedures linked to museum institutions in the historic center. However, opening hours and routes listed on information pages may change due to government operations. Confirm access for the particular date, especially if you want to see the murals, interior courtyards or historic rooms.

If entry is not possible on your chosen day, a walk across the [Zócalo](/mexico/place/mexico-city-zocalo/) still offers views of the facade and the palace's position in the city plan. The [Mexico City Metropolitan Cathedral](/mexico/place/mexico-city-metropolitan-cathedral/) stands on the square's northern side, with [Templo Mayor](/mexico/place/templo-mayor/) and the [Old Archbishop's Palace](/mexico/place/old-archbishop-palace/) in nearby streets.

### How is the palace different from neighboring museums?

The National Palace is an active government complex containing Rivera's murals. The Old Archbishop's Palace on Moneda Street is **a separate building** housing an art museum run by Mexico's Ministry of Finance. The names sometimes appear together because of the institutions' intertwined histories, but the collections and visiting arrangements differ. Be sure to confirm the exact address of each site.

## The National Palace on Ada Tours itineraries

Our [seven-day religious journey through Mexico](/mexico/tour/mexico-religious-journey/) lists the National Palace on the third day's route through historic Mexico City. The program also includes the [Zócalo](/mexico/place/mexico-city-zocalo/), [cathedral](/mexico/place/mexico-city-metropolitan-cathedral/), [Old Archbishop's Palace](/mexico/place/old-archbishop-palace/) and [Garibaldi Plaza](/mexico/place/garibaldi-plaza/). **Entry to the palace's interior depends on current access arrangements**; its facade and the surrounding streets can be viewed on the walking tour regardless.

Other cultural itineraries are available in [Mexico tours](/mexico/tour/) and [Culture and History trips](/interests/culture-and-history/tours/mexico/). The contents of any interior visits depend on the tour you choose.

## Frequently asked questions about the National Palace in Mexico City

### Where is the National Palace?

On the eastern side of Constitution Square, commonly known as the Zócalo, in historic Mexico City. It lies in the capital's center near the cathedral and Templo Mayor.

### Can all visitors see Diego Rivera's murals?

Access is not guaranteed on every day. Guided routes to the murals have historically been available, but the building remains a seat of government. Confirm advance registration requirements and entry availability before visiting.

### Can I see the palace without a guided tour?

Yes. Its main facade is clearly visible from the open Zócalo. Visiting the interior is subject to separate rules.

### How does the National Palace differ from the Old Archbishop's Palace?

The National Palace houses government departments and Rivera's murals. The [Old Archbishop's Palace](/mexico/place/old-archbishop-palace/) is a separate historic building with an art museum and archaeological evidence of earlier structures.
